newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Khariton, father of Soviet atom bomb dies at 92.
newsitem.headline: Khariton, father of Soviet atom bomb dies at 92.

text.p: Yuli Khariton, the Cambridge-educated nuclear physicist widely regarded as the father of the Soviet atom bomb, died on Thursday at the age of 92, Russian news agencies said.
Interfax said Khariton's body will be flown from the town of Sarov in central Russia where he died to Moscow to be buried at the capital's elite Novodevichye cemetery.

Khariton, one of Russia's most honoured and decorated scientists, often said the greatest moment of his life came on August 29, 1949 when the first Soviet atom bomb was tested near Semipalatinsk in Kazakhstan. Four years later, in October 1953 the Soviet Union tested its first hydrogen bomb.
Half a century later the history of the bombs, Moscow's Cold War challenge to the United States, is still shrouded in mist.
Khariton admitted his research centre at Sarov, then known as Arzamas-16, had made extensive use of intelligence on the U.S nuclear project provided by western atom spies like Klaus Fuchs.
But he always insisted Moscow's bomb was mostly the result of the work of Russian scientists.

During his long career in science, which started in 1925 when the ambitious youngster graduated from the Polytechnic Institute in St Petersburg, Khariton was lucky to escape the perils which claimed the lives of many of his collegues.

From 1926 to 1928 the Soviet government, keen to breed a new generation of loyal communist researchers and engineers to replace those who fled in the years of revolution and civil war, sent Khariton among others to study under British nuclear pioneer Ernest Rutherford at Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory.
The young Russian received his doctorate there.
A few years later many of those who had studied or worked in the West were to die in a string of political purges launched by dictator Josef Stalin. But Khariton escaped.
Together with Yakov Zeldovich, in 1939, he made calculations of the chain reaction triggered by the splitting of atoms of uranium, laying the basis for all further nuclear projects.

In April 1946, Khariton arrived in Sarov, then a sleepy town of 3,000, to found what would become one of the biggest Soviet nuclear research centres -- a top secret closed city where scientists lived and worked for decades in a privileged but tightly guarded world.
Khariton, who headed Arzamas-16 for more than 45 years, was a three-time winner of the title of Hero of Socialist Labour, the Soviet Union's highest civilian award.
